flagged.evidence: The claim quantifies over every $a\in[0,1)$, including $a=0$. Take $\hbar=m=q=1$, $A=(1,0,0)$ constant, and $\Phi=0$, which are admissible data. Then $K_{A,0}-K_0=-P_1+\tfrac12 I$. By the in-scope momentum lemma, $P_1$ is the Fourier multiplier $2\pi\xi_1$. Unit vectors whose Fourier transforms are supported in $[n,n+1]\times[0,1]^2$ belong to $W^{2,2}$ and have $\|(K_{A,0}-K_0)u_n\|\ge 2\pi n-\tfrac12$. Thus no finite $b$ gives the asserted inequality for $a=0$.

The cited gauge-domain result says each $G(t)$ preserves $W^{2,2}$ and that $t\mapsto G(t)h$ is continuous for fixed $h\in L^2$; it does not assert continuity in the $W^{2,2}$ norm. Proof 3.2 nevertheless infers from [F2] that $\varphi(t)=G(t)^{-1}v(t)$ is continuous into $W^{2,2}$. The gap occurs under the stated hypotheses: for nonzero $q$, choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ and $\chi(x,t)=t^2\eta(x_1)\sin(x_1/t)$ for $t\ne0$, $\chi(x,0)=0$. On $I=(-1,1)$ this has uniformly bounded first and second spatial derivatives and bounded pointwise time derivative, but $D_1^2\chi$ contains $-\eta(x_1)\sin(x_1/t)$, which does not converge strongly in $L^2$ when multiplied by a smooth $f$ with $\eta f\ne0$. Hence the claimed $W^{2,2}$ continuity does not follow. Uniqueness can instead be shown by differentiating the norm of the difference of the transformed $L^2$ solutions, so this proof gap is nonfatal.
